paragraphs: Bayesian learning can require sampling from distributions with several distinct peaks. The paper introduces contour stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics, or CSGLD, to make this sampling easier in large-data settings. It extends SGLD with weights that adapt during the simulation, making the method a scalable form of dynamic importance sampling.

The central idea is to automatically flatten the target distribution. This changes the landscape explored by the simulation so that sampling a distribution with multiple modes can be greatly facilitated. The method also uses weighted averaging estimators, and the paper analyzes the errors of those estimators alongside the adaptation mechanism.

The theoretical results include a stability condition and asymptotic convergence of the adapting parameter to a unique fixed point, despite possible nonconvexity of the original energy function. This is specifically a result about the adaptive parameter. Experiments on benchmark datasets, including CIFAR10 and CIFAR100, indicate advantages over the compared state-of-the-art algorithms for training deep neural networks, connecting the sampling proposal to practical Bayesian learning.
neurips-2020-a-contour-stochastic-gradie.tldr: CSGLD adaptively flattens multimodal distributions to facilitate scalable Bayesian sampling, with convergence analysis and promising neural-network experiments.

paragraphs: This paper builds neural network layers whose computations have an explicit optimization interpretation. A forward pass can be understood as solving a nonsmooth convex problem, and the layer architecture comes from an optimization algorithm. This connects the structure of a trainable model to a mathematical description of what its computations accomplish.

The framework focuses on convex games played by local agents arranged as nodes of a graph. Regularization functions govern how those agents interact. For imaging, this provides a way to incorporate established image priors into models trained end to end. The examples include total variation, Laplacian regularization, bilateral filtering, learned sparse dictionaries, and similarities between distant image regions.

The authors describe the resulting models as interpretable and efficient in their use of parameters and data. Their experiments cover image denoising, compressed sensing for fMRI, and dense stereo matching. The range of applications supports the framework's flexibility: different imaging assumptions can shape the model's computations while its parameters remain learnable from data.
neurips-2020-a-flexible-framework-for-de.tldr: The framework turns convex optimization and image priors into interpretable neural layers that can be trained end to end.

paragraphs: Object detection requires both recognizing objects and locating them accurately. The paper introduces average Localisation-Recall-Precision, or aLRP, as a single loss for training both capabilities. It develops a ranking-based objective from the LRP performance metric, extending an approach previously used by AP Loss for classification.

Using ranking for both tasks connects the ordering of predictions to their localization quality. The loss therefore encourages highly ranked, precise classifications to have accurate locations as well. The authors also prove balance between positive and negative examples. Its bounded, unified design uses one hyperparameter, which they leave untuned in practice, compared with roughly six on average in the detector losses discussed.

On COCO, aLRP improves over AP Loss by up to about five AP points and reaches 48.9 AP without test-time augmentation. The authors report outperforming all one-stage detectors in their comparison. These findings show how jointly structuring the two training objectives can improve reported detection performance while reducing the number of loss settings requiring attention.
neurips-2020-a-ranking-based-balanced-lo.tldr: aLRP unifies classification and localization through a balanced ranking loss, improving reported detection results with one untuned hyperparameter.

paragraphs: The paper develops a common mathematical framework for studying whether Q-learning algorithms converge. Its starting point is the nonlinear ordinary differential equations associated with Q-learning and several variants. The authors show that these equations can be represented as affine switching systems, allowing their behavior to be analyzed through a shared dynamical-systems perspective.

The key connection is between asymptotic stability of those systems and convergence of the learning algorithms. This representation supports a simpler differential-equation analysis of asynchronous Q-learning under relatively weak assumptions. The framework also yields what the authors identify as the first convergence analysis for averaging Q-learning, extending the usefulness of the same mathematical viewpoint.

For Q-learning with linear function approximation, the paper derives a new sufficient condition for convergence. That qualification matters: the result provides a condition that guarantees convergence when satisfied, without claiming it is necessary. The contribution is thus both organizational and analytical, bringing multiple variants into one framework while producing distinct convergence results for each.
neurips-2020-a-unified-switching-system-.tldr: A switching-system formulation unifies convergence analysis for several Q-learning variants and yields a new sufficient condition for linear approximation.

paragraphs: Observational data generally cannot fully determine a causal model. Experiments can improve identification, but their value depends on what is changed and how. Because experiments can be costly, this paper studies how to select interventions that efficiently reveal the direct causes of a particular response variable.

The proposed framework, Active Invariant Causal Prediction, builds experiment selection around Invariant Causal Prediction. Its theoretical foundation characterizes how interventions affect stable sets in general structural causal models. These results provide a basis for deciding which intervention to perform, linking the choice of experiment to stability properties relevant to causal discovery.

The authors use this analysis to develop several intervention-selection policies that quickly reveal direct causes while retaining ICP's error control. They evaluate the policies in both population and finite-data experiments. The contribution connects experimental planning with controlled causal inference: the framework aims to make each intervention informative without abandoning the error guarantees of the underlying prediction method.
neurips-2020-active-invariant-causal-pre.tldr: A-ICP uses intervention-induced stability changes to select informative causal experiments while preserving ICP's error control.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization and sampling depend on gradient estimates whose variability can slow progress. Importance sampling addresses this by changing how terms in a finite sum are selected. This paper develops an adaptive strategy for that selection, focusing on algorithms whose step sizes decrease as they run.

The method builds on a formulation of importance sampling as online learning with bandit feedback. Earlier work provided sublinear static regret; here, the authors analyze dynamic regret, addressing a comparison that can change over time. Their approach combines knowledge of the optimization or sampling dynamics with ideas from online learning and variance reduction.

Under standard technical conditions and step sizes of order 1/t, the algorithm achieves dynamic regret of order T^(2/3) for SGD and T^(5/6) for SGLD. These are guarantees for the adaptive sampling strategy under the specified conditions. Empirical results also identify settings with significant improvements, supporting the practical value of adapting sampling probabilities as the underlying algorithm evolves.
neurips-2020-adaptive-importance-samplin.tldr: An adaptive importance sampler obtains sublinear dynamic regret for SGD and SGLD with decreasing step sizes under stated technical conditions.

paragraphs: Online learning with bandit feedback must make decisions using only partial information about losses. This paper studies guarantees against an adaptive adversary and develops a way to bound regret with high probability. The bounds depend on the observed problem data, so they can be substantially smaller than worst-case guarantees.

The approach uses standard unbiased loss estimators together with an increasing learning-rate schedule. Its analysis combines specialized mathematical barriers with a strengthened version of Freedman's inequality. This supplies an alternative to earlier approaches that required carefully designed optimistic, biased estimators to obtain high-probability guarantees.

The framework yields what the authors identify as the first general, efficient algorithm with a high-probability regret bound for adversarial linear bandits. It also extends to adversarial Markov decision processes, producing a high-probability small-loss bound. Together, these results resolve the open problems described in the abstract and show that unbiased estimation can support strong, data-sensitive guarantees across multiple partial-feedback learning settings.
neurips-2020-bias-no-more-high-probabili.tldr: Unbiased estimators and increasing learning rates yield high-probability, data-dependent regret guarantees for adversarial bandits and MDPs.

paragraphs: BOSS tackles Bayesian optimization when candidate inputs are strings, potentially with different lengths and strict syntax. Existing approaches discussed in the paper first learn a mapping from strings into a smooth, unconstrained latent space. Building that mapping can require substantial data and computation, creating an additional burden before optimization can proceed effectively.

The proposed method works directly with raw strings. It constructs a Gaussian process surrogate using string kernels and uses genetic algorithms within the Bayesian optimization loop. The kernel-based surrogate naturally accommodates variable-length inputs, while the acquisition optimization procedure searches spaces subject to syntactic restrictions.

Experiments show considerably better optimization than existing approaches across a broad range of constraints, including syntax specified by a context-free grammar. The result supports direct string modeling as a useful alternative to learning a latent projection. Its significance is the combination of a string-aware predictive model and an efficient search procedure that can respect the structure of valid candidates.
neurips-2020-boss-bayesian-optimization-.tldr: BOSS combines string kernels and genetic search to optimize raw, variable-length strings under syntactic constraints.

paragraphs: This paper approaches continual learning by adapting the activation maps of a CNN already trained on an earlier task. It shows that a small collection of calibration parameters can make those activations useful for a new task. Spatial and channel-wise calibration modules perform this adaptation at each network layer.

For each new task, training updates only its calibration parameters. The method stores those parameters separately for each task, preserving the task-specific knowledge and avoiding catastrophic forgetting through that separation. It also avoids retaining old training examples. Compared with approaches that dynamically expand the network, the calibration modules require substantially fewer additional parameters and computations.

Experiments across SVHN, CIFAR, ImageNet, and MS-Celeb show substantial improvements over the compared methods. Reported gains include a 29% absolute accuracy increase on CIFAR-100 when learning ten classes at a time. On ImageNet-100 and MS-Celeb-10K, the reported absolute gains are 23.8% and 9.7%, using calibration parameters amounting to 0.51% and 0.35% of model parameters, respectively.
neurips-2020-calibrating-cnns-for-lifelo.tldr: Small, separately stored calibration modules adapt CNN activations to new tasks while preserving earlier task knowledge without replay data.

paragraphs: Collapsing Bandits model decisions where taking an action also reveals the state of the thing being acted on. Each arm follows a binary-state Markov process. Playing it reveals its state completely; leaving it passive produces no observation, so uncertainty evolves. A limited action budget must keep as many arms as possible in the good state.

This matches healthcare settings where workers both monitor patients and deliver interventions. The authors build on Whittle indices and derive conditions under which the problem is indexable. Their analysis characterizes when optimal policies can have forward or reverse threshold forms, then exploits that structure to compute indices efficiently, including through a closed-form expression.

Evaluations use several data distributions, including data concerning adherence to tuberculosis medication. The algorithm achieves a three-order-of-magnitude speedup over the compared RMAB techniques while maintaining similar performance. The contribution combines a model of observation-dependent uncertainty with conditional structural results that make intervention planning much faster in the tested settings.
neurips-2020-collapsing-bandits-and-thei.tldr: Collapsing Bandits model actions that reveal hidden states and use threshold-policy structure to accelerate budgeted intervention planning.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can be expensive to execute, and available computing devices increasingly differ in their capabilities. This paper studies how to divide a network's computation graph among multiple devices. Its focus includes pipelined execution, where a stream of samples passes through successive devices to support high training or inference throughput.

The authors isolate a structured optimization problem underlying the placement of individual neural-network operators. This makes device assignment a precisely defined problem for automated algorithms and toolchains. They address both inference and training, with particular attention to the requirements of large models running across heterogeneous hardware.

The paper provides algorithms that solve the formulated placement problem to optimality and demonstrates their applicability and efficiency on several contemporary DNN computation graphs. The optimality claim concerns that structured optimization problem. The practical significance is a systematic way to determine how a model should be partitioned for pipelined model parallelism, supporting automated placement as models and hardware combinations become more complex.
neurips-2020-efficient-algorithms-for-de.tldr: The paper formulates pipelined DNN device placement as a structured optimization problem and provides algorithms that solve it optimally.

paragraphs: Gradient clipping is widely used to manage exploding gradients during neural-network training. Earlier theory showed advantages over ordinary gradient descent under an assumption called (L0, L1)-smoothness, designed to capture sharp changes in gradients. However, those bounds had pessimistic dependence on problem parameters and did not adequately explain clipping combined with momentum.

This paper develops a general framework that includes both clipping and momentum methods. It analyzes convergence in deterministic and stochastic settings, covering computations with exact gradients and those using noisy estimates. The authors assess the tightness of their results by comparing the guarantees with existing lower bounds.

Within the analyzed framework, the results imply that clipping methods retain their efficiency even in regions where the landscape behaves highly nonsmoothly. Deep-learning experiments also favor clipping-based methods. The contribution strengthens the mathematical explanation for a practical training technique and extends that explanation to its interaction with momentum, rather than analyzing clipping only as an isolated modification.
neurips-2020-improved-analysis-of-clippi.tldr: A unified analysis strengthens convergence guarantees for gradient clipping and incorporates momentum in deterministic and stochastic optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies how well kernel ridge regression generalizes when observations are independent and identically distributed and ridge regularization is positive. It introduces a Signal Capture Threshold to describe which components of the data the predictor captures. That threshold also supports an approximation of expected generalization error.

The analysis leads to the Kernel Alignment Risk Estimator, or KARE, which is computed explicitly from training data without knowing the true data distribution. The mathematical development adapts a random-matrix resolvent method to finite sizes. Results for the predictor's mean and variance rely on a universality assumption: asymptotically, the relevant moments depend on the observations' first two moments.

Numerical investigations on Higgs and MNIST with several classical kernels find that KARE closely approximates risk, supporting the proposed universality hypothesis. This makes KARE promising for comparing kernels and hyperparameters directly from the training set. The finding is an empirically supported risk approximation with an assumption-based theoretical foundation, offering a data-dependent route to model selection.
neurips-2020-kernel-alignment-risk-estim.tldr: KARE estimates kernel ridge regression's generalization error from training data, supported by conditional theory and numerical evidence.

paragraphs: Sensory neural populations have limited capacity because neurons, biological resources, and reliable signals are all constrained. This paper explores how a circuit could learn to preserve information that matters for its task while using those resources efficiently. It constructs a stochastic recurrent neural model with a new reward-modulated Hebbian rule for changing synaptic connections.

The authors train an initially unstructured network on two different tasks: estimating stimuli and discriminating between them. The model achieves high performance on both by allocating its resources appropriately. Its recurrent connections also help compensate for different noise levels, connecting the circuit's learned organization to the reliability of its inputs and activity.

The study further shows that the resulting representations depend jointly on stimulus priors and task structure. What the network represents therefore reflects both which stimuli commonly occur and what distinctions the task requires. The model supplies a computational account of how synaptic learning can produce efficient, task-dependent sensory codes under resource and noise constraints.
neurips-2020-learning-efficient-task-dep.tldr: A recurrent neural circuit learns efficient sensory representations through reward-modulated plasticity, adapting to task demands, stimulus priors, and noise.

paragraphs: Variational inference approximates a posterior distribution p using a tractable distribution q. Most methods choose q by minimizing KL(q||p), partly because that direction is computationally convenient. This paper instead targets KL(p||q), the inclusive divergence, whose statistical properties make it better suited to certain inference problems.

The proposed algorithm, Markovian score climbing, uses stochastic gradients with bias that vanishes. It converges to a local optimum of the inclusive divergence. The authors distinguish this from existing methods such as Reweighted Wake-Sleep and Neural Adaptive Sequential Monte Carlo, whose systematic errors can leave bias in their final estimates.

The paper illustrates convergence on a toy model and demonstrates the method on Bayesian probit classification and a stochastic volatility model for financial data. These examples connect its convergence properties to practical inference tasks. The guarantee concerns a local optimum within the chosen approximating family, providing a reliable way to optimize the inclusive objective without claiming recovery of the exact posterior.
neurips-2020-markovian-score-climbing-va.tldr: Markovian score climbing minimizes inclusive KL divergence using stochastic gradients with vanishing bias and converges to a local optimum.

paragraphs: Claims that some model families are easier to interpret often lack a formal basis for comparison. This paper proposes measuring interpretability through the computational difficulty of answering post-hoc explanation queries. The queries concern why a model assigns a particular classification to an individual input.

Under this definition, one model class is more interpretable when answering the relevant queries is computationally easier than for another class. Assuming standard complexity-theoretic conjectures such as P not equaling NP, the authors prove that linear and tree-based models are strictly more interpretable than neural networks. The conclusion is tied to the paper's computational definition of explanation difficulty.

The analysis does not establish one fixed ordering between linear and tree-based models: their relative difficulty changes with the explanation query. A finer analysis using parameterized complexity also yields a result suggesting that shallow networks are more interpretable than deeper ones. Together, these findings give familiar intuitions a theoretical counterpart while showing that the kind of explanation requested matters.
neurips-2020-model-interpretability-thro.tldr: The paper formalizes interpretability through explanation-query complexity, deriving conditional comparisons between linear models, trees, and neural networks.

paragraphs: Neural Sparse Voxel Fields address the cost and quality of rendering a scene from new viewpoints. Earlier implicit scene representations can produce blurry images and require expensive ray marching. NSVF divides the representation into local implicit fields bounded by voxels, organized in a sparse octree.

The system progressively learns the voxel structure using differentiable ray marching from RGB images with known camera poses. It therefore learns the scene without requiring direct 3D supervision. During rendering, the sparse structure allows rays to skip voxels that contain no relevant scene content, reducing computation spent traversing uninformative space.

The authors report rendering more than ten times faster than the state of the art while producing higher-quality results. The explicit voxel structure also supports scene editing and composition. Demonstrations include learning multiple objects, rendering a moving human from different viewpoints, and handling large scenes. These results connect local neural representations with spatial structure that is useful both for rendering efficiency and for manipulating scenes.
neurips-2020-neural-sparse-voxel-fields-.tldr: NSVF learns local neural fields in a sparse voxel structure, accelerating novel-view rendering by skipping space without relevant content.

paragraphs: This paper studies distributed online optimization when communication between computing nodes is random. At each step, every node chooses a local decision, incurs a convex loss, and communicates with other nodes. Each potential link in a prescribed connected graph independently appears with probability p.

The authors analyze distributed gradient methods with full-gradient feedback and with one-point or two-point bandit information, covering convex and strongly convex losses. Their regret bounds describe dependence on the time horizon, number of nodes, decision dimension, and algebraic network connectivity. This connects optimization performance to both the feedback available and the communication structure.

The time dependence matches the corresponding centralized rates discussed in the paper, including square-root and logarithmic regret in the specified settings. For networks permitting all-to-all communication, the authors also derive how the bounds depend on p. This makes the tradeoff between communication overhead and optimization accuracy explicit. Numerical studies support the theoretical findings, showing how random connectivity can be incorporated into performance analysis.
neurips-2020-online-convex-optimization-.tldr: The paper quantifies how random communication affects distributed online optimization and exposes a tradeoff between communication cost and accuracy.

paragraphs: Parametric Instance Classification, or PIC, learns visual features without labels through a single-branch classification framework. The approach resembles supervised classification in its structure, while treating instances as the classification targets. It offers an alternative to the dual-branch, nonparametric instance-discrimination approaches discussed in the paper.

The authors show that PIC can match the effectiveness of SimCLR and MoCo v2 after adopting several common component settings. They also introduce a sliding-window data scheduler to address the extremely infrequent revisiting of instances under an epoch-based schedule. This change improves effectiveness by modifying how training examples are encountered over time.

A second technique combines negative sampling with weight-update correction to reduce training time and GPU memory consumption. The authors state that this enables application to almost unlimited training images. Together, these changes make the simple classification formulation more practical at scale. The paper positions PIC as a useful baseline for studying unsupervised visual learning, supported by competitive results and targeted improvements to scheduling and computational cost.
neurips-2020-parametric-instance-classif.tldr: PIC offers a competitive single-branch approach to unsupervised visual learning, with scheduling and sampling improvements that reduce training costs.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover a leading covariance direction when a fraction of the samples has been corrupted. The uncorrupted data comes from a sub-Gaussian distribution. The goal is an approximate top eigenvector, giving useful information about the covariance despite the contaminated observations.

The authors provide two algorithms with different tradeoffs. An iterative filtering method runs in polynomial time and obtains an approximation factor of 1 minus a term of order epsilon times log(1/epsilon). A second method achieves a slightly weaker approximation but uses nearly linear time and sample complexity under a mild spectral-gap assumption.

The authors identify these as the first polynomial-time methods obtaining nontrivial covariance information in this setting without additional algebraic structure in the moments. A key technical contribution is a family of width-independent solvers for Schatten-p packing semidefinite programs. Those solvers provide approximate solutions using input-sparsity-time iterations, linking the robust statistical guarantees to advances in the efficiency of the underlying matrix optimization.
neurips-2020-robust-sub-gaussian-princip.tldr: Two robust PCA algorithms estimate leading covariance directions from corrupted sub-Gaussian samples, with a faster method requiring a mild spectral gap.

paragraphs: This paper examines the geometry of gradient-based adversarial attacks on Bayesian neural networks. Its theoretical setting is the limit of large datasets and overparameterized models. The analysis connects vulnerability to the shape of the data distribution, particularly cases where data occupies a lower-dimensional submanifold within the surrounding input space.

In that limiting setting, the authors show that vulnerability to gradient-based attacks arises from this degeneracy of the data distribution. They then establish robustness of Bayesian neural-network posteriors to those attacks in the limit. Both the asymptotic setting and the restriction to gradient-based attacks are central to the stated theoretical result.

Experiments on MNIST and Fashion MNIST use Bayesian networks trained through Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and variational inference. The results support the theoretical argument by showing that these models can combine high accuracy with resistance to gradient-based attacks. The contribution connects a geometric explanation of vulnerability with posterior-based robustness and empirical evidence in the evaluated classification settings.
neurips-2020-robustness-of-bayesian-neur.tldr: The paper establishes limiting robustness of Bayesian neural-network posteriors to gradient-based attacks and reports supporting classification experiments.

paragraphs: Sparse Weight Activation Training, or SWAT, aims to reduce the computation and memory required to train convolutional networks. It builds on an empirical observation: training convergence tends to tolerate removing small-magnitude weights during the forward pass and removing both small weights and small activations during the backward pass.

The algorithm modifies backpropagation to exploit this tolerance. Evaluations cover ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, and WideResNet on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The approach is intended to benefit hardware designed to accelerate sparse computations, connecting reduced arithmetic and storage requirements to the capabilities of emerging platforms.

For ResNet-50 on ImageNet, SWAT reduces training FLOPs by 80% with a reported 1.63% reduction in validation accuracy. A simulated sparse learning accelerator yields a 3.3-fold training speedup; that timing result specifically concerns the simulated hardware. The paper also reports backward-pass memory reductions of 23–50% for activations and 50–90% for weights, showing substantial resource savings with an evaluated accuracy tradeoff.
neurips-2020-sparse-weight-activation-tr.tldr: SWAT reduces CNN training computation and memory by omitting small weights and activations, with measured accuracy tradeoffs and simulated accelerator speedups.

paragraphs: StratLearner asks whether a strategy for a combinatorial problem can be learned from input-solution examples without knowing the objective function. Its application is misinformation prevention: given examples pairing attackers with protectors, the method learns to choose protectors against future attackers without access to the underlying diffusion model.

The proposed structured-prediction framework learns a scoring function for these decisions. It constructs random features from distance functions on randomly sampled subgraphs, producing a kernelized score whose weights are learned through a large-margin method. This uses graph structure and example solutions to guide future choices without explicitly modeling how misinformation spreads.

Experiments show that the method can produce near-optimal protectors without diffusion-model information and outperforms the compared graph-based and learning-based alternatives by a clear margin. Those findings support learning a prevention strategy directly from examples in the evaluated settings. More broadly, the paper demonstrates an instance of learning optimization behavior when successful input-solution pairs are available but the objective governing them is unknown.
neurips-2020-stratlearner-learning-a-str.tldr: StratLearner learns misinformation-protection strategies from attacker-protector examples using graph features, without knowing the diffusion model.

paragraphs: This paper builds a model of how the inner retina processes visual information over time. It incorporates inhibitory feedback involving amacrine cells and realistic mechanisms for synaptic release. These biological structures are often absent from strong black-box CNN models, despite detailed knowledge of retinal cell types and circuits.

The researchers fit the model to bipolar-cell responses and test it on new stimuli, including natural movies. It generalizes well, matching or exceeding a benchmark black-box model. This shows that the incorporated biological structure can coexist with strong predictive performance in the evaluated temporal-processing tasks.

The model also reproduces the effects of pharmacologically blocking specific amacrine-cell populations with high fidelity. That agreement indicates that it learned important circuit functions. Separately, learned connectivity patterns align well with patterns extracted from connectomics data. Together, these checks support a biologically interpretable, data-driven account of inner-retinal processing, connecting response prediction with evidence about circuit interventions and anatomical organization.
neurips-2020-system-identification-with-.tldr: A biologically constrained retinal model predicts new responses and reproduces intervention effects while learning connectivity consistent with anatomical data.

paragraphs: Adding Gaussian noise is a common way to protect sensitive data through differential privacy. Continuous noise creates an implementation challenge because finite computers cannot represent continuous samples exactly. The abstract notes that numerical errors can destroy privacy guarantees. Continuous outputs can also be awkward to interpret when the original query produces an integer count.

This paper introduces and analyzes discrete Gaussian noise for differential privacy. The authors show theoretically and experimentally that it provides essentially the same privacy and accuracy guarantees as continuous Gaussian noise. This preserves the main benefits of the Gaussian mechanism while working with a distribution suited to discrete outputs.

The paper also supplies a simple, efficient algorithm that samples exactly from the discrete distribution. Exact sampling directly addresses the numerical representation concern motivating the work. The results establish applicability to private counting queries and, more generally, integer-valued queries with low sensitivity, connecting mathematical privacy analysis to a concrete mechanism that finite computers can implement.
neurips-2020-the-discrete-gaussian-for-d.tldr: Discrete Gaussian noise offers essentially continuous-Gaussian privacy and accuracy guarantees with efficient exact sampling for integer-valued queries.
